newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda trial hears accused ordered killing.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda trial hears accused ordered killing.

text.p: The U.N. Rwanda tribunal heard on Thursday how a vice-president of the extremist Interahamwe militia accused of genocide ordered ethnic Tutsis killed, but the defense disputed the evidence.

Witness "M", so-called to protect his identity, said he saw accused Georges Rutaganda distribute weapons to the militia near a well in the Rwandan capital Kigali shortly after the start of the genocide.

"When I arrived at the well Rutaganda had arrived. He was wearing a soldier's uniform and was accompanied by about six Interahamwe. The Interahamwe were wearing civilian uniform with a white bullet-proof vest only worn by Belgian soldiers," witness M said.
"I heard him tell the Interahamwe to go and kill the Tutsis out there otherwise he was going to bring an armoured tank to exterminate them (militiamen)," he said.
But Rutaganda's defense counsel Tiphaine Dickson said the testimony contradicted a signed statement witness "M" made to tribunal investigators in 1995.

"I recently told you to forgive me because the statement was made two years ago and I don't remember it very well...I only remember the events of 1994. I don't remember any events of 1995 at all even if they were written," witness "M" told the court.
The non-disclosure to the court of the earlier evidence was "a serious violation of procedure", Dickson told court president Laity Kama of Senegal.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) was set up in 1994 to bring to trial the leading architects of the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus sparked by the assassination of Rwanda's President Juvenal Habyarimana.
So far 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal, plagued by administrative and financial problems. A total of 12 suspects are in detention in Arusha, northern Tanzania.
